A clarification is essential. The cardinality $|\mathcal{C}_D|$ of the deep hidden sector is *gauge* in the framework: different values of $|\mathcal{C}_D|$ produce the same visible transition data exactly for a deep sector beyond the reach of the dynamics over the times considered, and at leading order on accessible timescales under the posited influence bound H-BD of [GR §3.2]. The "total information" of the universe is therefore not fixed by those data. But the *finiteness* of $|\mathcal{C}_D|$ — for the recurrence route specifically, that there exists some finite value, even if its specific magnitude is not observable — is load-bearing. Infinite hidden sectors would break the recurrence argument that drives recurrence-scale P-indivisibility; that route would close. P-indivisibility itself does not require finite $S$: any revival of distinguishability between the visible laws of two roots implies it, whatever the size of the hidden sector. For the selected linear update on the infinite lattice, with prime $q$, a nonzero coupling coefficient, a uniform product prior on the hidden sites and lattice-convex visible windows, no such revival occurs, and the process is P-divisible at every horizon. Accessible non-Markovianity would survive through readback, and the imported representation is gated by (T) rather than by recurrence, so an infinite substratum removes this route rather than the framework's quantum representation.
Second, A1 can also hold on a finite lattice region with prescribed boundary conditions and finitely many states per site.

**Framework status.** The horizon first law and boundary count give the thermal energy used in the comparison. Its Hubble-volume mean is $\rho_s=3c^2H^2/(8\pi G)$ in three spatial dimensions, equal to the supplied flat Friedmann density. The equality concerns the average. The physical source requires the open covariant coupling. [GR §7.2]

**Framework status.** Split — fixed-basis representation settled exactly; coherent operational extension characterized by five conditions. Every finite-horizon stochastic law has an exact fixed-basis unitary/Born representation ($S\iff D\iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}$, [Main §3.4]); in that theorem the quadratic Born dictionary is part of the equivalent representation, not a separate exponent-selection problem. The further question begins when one asks for **one common operational theory** covering arbitrary coherent preparations, noncommuting effects/instruments, and composites. Main's finite response table realizes the supplied quantum probabilities for a fixed preparation, instrument menu and horizon. The finite instrument net extends coverage to arbitrary finite accuracy at fixed initial state. The same response-table machinery can also realize non-quantum finite behaviors. The operational-completion characterization ([GR §3.3]) states exactly which conditions select the quantum ones — valid probabilities, trivial-ancilla consistency, inert spectators, full reversible control, and iterated composition — each independent of the others and of the observation process, so that embedded observation by itself does not select quantum mechanics and the physical question is which of those conditions the substratum supplies. The characterization takes complex matrix kinematics as given — operations act on the complex matrices indexed by the configurations of the system and of its composites — and deriving that kinematics is a further open question. Its layered form, quantum-complete OI (OI⁺) — the unchanged OI core with well-formedness, observational independence, reversible richness, and observer recursion — is equivalent on every nonempty finite carrier to exact finite endomorphic operational quantum mechanics, with no claim that bare OI entails the added principles ([GR §3.3]). A primitive-source refinement of that layered form restates the three principles at the level of physical implementations and embedded observers — implementation locality, phase-free richness — one continuously driven transition and the exchanges of distinguishable states, with no phase operation — and embedded observation, with no closure of the implementations under the adjoint and no inverse accessibility assumed — equivalent to the same operational quantum mechanics on every nonempty finite carrier ([GR §3.3]). A substratum-source form completes that refinement: the concrete OI substratum, in its finite model (ledger item (ii)), supplies the structural architecture — closure under composition and coarse-graining, stability under an uncoupled spectator, relabelling invariance, reversibility, the exchanges of distinguishable states, and, as a stated intervention principle rather than a consequence of its finite states and bijective dynamics, the phases — but, under finite bijective read-write dynamics as represented by the specified monomial implementation class, elementary drivability fails, and the generated theory on the two-state carrier lacks composite unitary control. A structurally closed extension with elementary drivability generates exact finite endomorphic operational quantum mechanics on every nonempty finite carrier. In the memory-swap example, a nontrivial exchange of the selected states has a monomial operator ([GR §3.3]). Its typed form removes the endomorphic qualifier: under the carrier-general typed operational interface — identity, composition, coarse-graining, relabelling, uniform finite attachment, discard, and factor readout, an interface that itself carries no quantum content — the same equivalence holds with exact finite-dimensional typed operational quantum mechanics, operations between any two nonempty finite carriers included, so the remaining qualifier is finite-dimensional rather than endomorphic ([GR §3.3]). The finite theory admits a canonical infinite-region completion without a continuum limit: the finite regions of the fixed-spacing lattice carry full matrix algebras joined by compatible injective unital embeddings with observables of disjoint regions commuting, the norm completion of their union is a quasilocal $C^{*}$-algebra on which every consistent family of finite-region density matrices is a state and the reversible finite-range substratum update is an isometric $*$-automorphism, and any system carrying the same local stages is canonically and uniquely $*$-isomorphic to it, intertwining the dynamics; this removes the finite-region cutoff for the algebra, the state space, and the OI-induced discrete dynamics rather than characterizing all infinite-dimensional quantum instruments or all locality-preserving quantum dynamics; the lattice spacing stays fundamental, no Hilbert-space representation and no superselection sector is selected at the level of the laws, the restriction to the substratum-induced dynamics is a theorem rather than a convention — a phase automorphism at one site preserves locality without arising from any reversible finite-range bijection — and, while the update is joined to the identity by an exact strongly continuous path of $*$-automorphisms of that algebra, with no one-parameter-group law established and no generator exhibited, a continuous-time Hamiltonian law remains additional structure ([GR §3.3]). Within the structural architecture the substratum supplies, with the phase intervention stated, exact finite endomorphic operational quantum mechanics holds exactly when one continuous layer flow of an involution of the configuration space moving some configuration is an available operation at every level and every intermediate time, the executability of that flow being an assumption not derived by configuration-level generation, as the phase intervention is an assumption on the substratum class and not a consequence of the finite states with the bijective dynamics ([GR §3.3]). The stated substratum dynamics with the observer's read and write access do not source that executability, the layers being available at time one and not at intermediate times, and the observer-level lift, in every formulation stated that lands in the operational interface, derives neither a non-monomial admissible operator nor the layer flow, the site-space wave-operator formulation being unresolved rather than excluded ([GR §3.3]). The cosmological realization adds a mechanism proposal — the equilibrium reading of the read-write cycle (Chapter 18 §18.2) — whose stationary-distribution step is a structural commitment rather than a premise of the representation theorem.

*The bottom-to-tau mass ratio.* The framework predicts $y_b = y_\tau$ at tree level — the staggered taste-breaking is diagonal in the gauge index. Full Standard Model RGE running (verified against Luo and Xiao 2003) gives $m_b/m_\tau|_{\text{tree}} = 4.276$ from a common $M_{\text{Pl}}$ boundary condition, indicating a substantial non-perturbative correction. The full prediction including the scalar-density renormalization $Z_S$ from non-perturbative dynamics at the matching scale is developed in Chapter 6 §6.6 (and SM §7.5): with matching scale $m_{\text{match}} = \lambda g_0^2 = 0.1217$ derived structurally from the taste-decomposed Coleman-Weinberg potential, and $Z_S(m_{\text{match}}) = 1.813$ measured from Monte Carlo at $\beta = 11.1$ on $L = 32$, the prediction is $m_b/m_\tau = 4.28/Z_S(m_{\text{match}}) = 2.361$ against the observed $2.352 \pm 0.017$ — a $0.4\%$ ($0.5\sigma$) match at $L = 32$, with $L \to \infty$ extrapolation giving $\sim 0.7\sigma$. The $L = 16$ Monte Carlo using only the $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ mass renormalization $Z_m \approx 0.835$ at fixed bare mass — the calculation described in earlier versions of this section as giving $\sim 3.4$ ($45\%$ off) — corresponds to using the wrong matching prescription rather than the wrong physics. With the correct matching scale (a structural feature of the taste-decomposed CW potential rather than a tunable parameter), the prediction matches observation at the same level as the framework's other Layer 1 closures (Cabibbo, Koide, $\sin^2\theta_{13}$). The kinematic prefactor $K = 1/(n_{\text{gen}} - 1) = 1/2$ is a Layer-1 structural identity given the matching condition ($c_{bb} = (n_{\text{gen}}-1)\lambda$); its support is the Monte Carlo verification at $1.4\%$ ($K_{\text{MC}} = 0.507$). The explicit one-loop evaluation has been carried out and cannot close the gap: in the condensate-ratio construction the one-loop coefficient is $0.446$ (tadpole-normalization bracket $0.393$–$0.446$), $11$–$21\%$ below $1/2$ at a coupling where $Z_S - 1 = 0.81$ — a truncation error an order of magnitude larger than the MC precision, indicting the truncation rather than the identity. Analytical closure requires the resummed staggered-χPT chain or a non-perturbative identity, or alternatively sub-percent MC; the task is Layer 2(a) in scope but not one-loop in method (SM §7.5).

*No inflation needed.* The framework's lattice structure may resolve the horizon and flatness problems differently. On a finite lattice, the notion of "causally disconnected regions" is modified — the lattice's coupling graph determines causal structure, and if the initial state of $\varphi$ is statistically isotropic (one of the framework's six structural properties of the bijection), isotropy is built in rather than requiring inflation to produce it. This is speculative and would require a detailed analysis of the lattice's causal structure at early times.

*Why this equivalence class rather than another.* The framework's axioms — deterministic bijectivity, causal partition, classical probability — together with the open hypothesis A1 of finiteness constrain the class. The framework's six structural properties of the bijection (developed across Chapters 5-7) further narrow it. But the axioms themselves are not derived from anything deeper.

The existence question — "why does $(S, \varphi)$ exist at all?" — is the framework's irreducible mystery. The framework's structural account: $(S, \varphi)$ is a mathematical structure that cannot fail to be well-defined; existence is the default for logically consistent structures. Whether one finds this answer satisfying is a philosophical question rather than a physical one. The framework's commitment is that the existence of *some* deterministic bijection structure (finite under A1) is not a question physics can answer, while the existence of *this particular* structure (as determined by the empirical record) is a constraint on which bijections are compatible with observation.

**Assessment.** The framework identifies this question as the only genuinely irreducible mystery — not a gap in the framework's reach but the boundary of all possible frameworks. Any framework must take some structural axioms as given; the framework's content is to make those axioms as minimal and as structural as possible (deterministic bijectivity, on a finite set under A1, no further commitments), leaving the existence question as an explicit acknowledgment of where physics ends.

Two results bear on this question. A symmetric-integration argument shows that an exactly $O_h$-invariant action, measure, and observer-centered partition yield an $O_h$-invariant effective theory to all orders, and every ingredient of the checkerboard trace-out is $O_h$-invariant — no direction-dependent momentum shell is available. A numerical check on the rounded interacting dynamics, whose code and numerical output are not available for verification (extraction reported validated against the analytic tree coefficients to the percent level; the allowed $\ell=4$ anisotropy reported detected at high significance), reported the forbidden $E_g$ coefficient zero within errors at the $2\times10^{-5}$ level in the perturbative regime and consistent with zero in the thermalized strong-coupling state. Separately, the sector-differential boost violation's custodial decoupling law — conditional on the symmetric-point matching under H-blind ([SM §4.4]) — has its normalization bounded ($\Delta C_2 \in [0.58, 2.08]$ from the framework's representation content), and its decoupling form, controls and kernel constants ($c_L \simeq -9.4$, $d \simeq -0.88$) reported by a one-loop calculation whose driver and numerical output are not available for verification; on that reported form the worst-case $\Delta C_2$ would give an $M_X$ window of two to five orders of magnitude against the tightest multi-species bounds, an intermediate scale $\lesssim 10^8$ GeV, narrowing with the reported constants and the representation-side point values to a ceiling of $\sim 4\times10^{7}$ GeV and a window of one and a half to four and a half decades — illustrative figures carrying the provenance of that calculation ([SM §3.1]). What remains: production-scale statistics, the $\ell=4$ alignment of the observer-position boundary anisotropy, and the cross-charged phenomenology floor. See [SM §3.1] for the full statements.

*Mathematics and logical foundations.* The framework presupposes standard mathematics (ZFC set theory, the integers, finite combinatorics) without addressing the foundations of mathematics. Whether the finiteness hypothesis A1 has implications for mathematical foundations (constructivism, finitism, ultrafinitism) is not addressed.

**A1 (Finiteness).** The open hypothesis, not adopted, that the substratum has a finite total configuration space (Chapter 2 §2.4), as assumed in the minimal finite representative. Motivated physically by the Bekenstein bound at the cosmological horizon (an entropy-based bound, under the physical assumptions of input E3, of at most $e^{S_{\text{dS}}}$ effectively distinguishable states of the visible sector and boundary layer, $S_{\text{dS}} \sim 10^{122}$). It is one sufficient condition for the results that use it, each of which names the hypotheses it consumes. Discussed in Chapter 2 §2.4, with defense in Appendix C §C.6.

**Background independence (A6).** The sixth of the framework's structural assumptions A1–A6: the substratum dynamics is covariant under spatially varying internal-index transformations, a site-dependent transformation being a symmetry provided the coupling data carried on the links are transformed with it. The content of the assumption is the covariant interface itself — the coupling is link-valued data the transformations act on — and once that is in place the local transformation law imposes no further condition on the rule. It is distinct from the stronger fixed-background condition that the same transformations leave the dynamics invariant with the coupling held fixed, which for an invertible coupling forces agreement across every coupled pair of sites; from the global commutant symmetry, its specialization to transformations constant across the lattice that leave the coupling unchanged, from which the local gauge reading proceeds; and from the state-dependent coupling graph, a separate principle sharing the name, under which the graph itself evolves with the state. Where the framework says it has no fixed spacetime background, with spacetime emergent, that is a third sense of the words and not this assumption. Developed in Chapter 2 §2.4 and Chapter 5 §5.5.

**Non-Markovian.** A stochastic process whose future depends on past states beyond the present. Accessible history dependence is the content of a C4 witness. Finite-alphabet and finite-horizon representability also holds for memoryless laws, and recurrence-scale P-indivisibility uses a non-permutation rooted map and a finite return ([Main §3.4]). Physical applications require their own witnesses. Defined in Chapter 1 §1.5. Three notions are kept apart throughout and none unconditionally implies another: *accessible finite-horizon memory* (equivalently conditional past–future dependence in the visible law) is the framework's own term and is what "non-Markovian on accessible horizons" means here; *stochastic P-indivisibility* is failure of divisibility of the visible population law and rests on recurrence together with a non-permutation rooted map, not on C1/C3/C4 alone; *generic quantum non-Markovianity* is an open-system notion whose content depends on the quantum divisibility or backflow criterion adopted, and it is not what either of the first two asserts.

**Substratum.** The underlying deterministic system $(S, \varphi)$, modelled by a bijection on total configurations. Its total configuration space is finite in the representative specified under the open posit A1. With a partition and preparation, tracing out the hidden sector gives a visible law with an exact fixed-basis quantum representation for finite alphabets and horizons. The substratum is the framework's primitive ontological commitment, held at the level of the reconstructed local residue modulo the substratum gauge group rather than any particular representative (Chapter 3) — the "what is really there" beneath the emergent quantum-mechanical description. Constructed concretely in Chapter 2.

This book argues a heterodox position: quantum mechanics may have an observer-level origin in incomplete observation. For supplied observable laws on finite alphabets and horizons, three descriptions coincide: stochastic laws, finite reversible deterministic realizations, and fixed-basis unitary/Born representations. The equivalence is bidirectional and exact on every finite horizon. History readback supplies the nontrivial content: it forces hidden predictive memory. In the finite reversible model with a common uniform hidden prior, a non-permutation rooted visible step implies P-indivisibility by the return, including for laws that are Markov on accessible windows. The book develops the consequences of taking that equivalence as a structural fact rather than as an interpretive analogy.

**Appendix C (Common Objections and Framework Responses).** Systematic engagement with the most predictable objections to the framework's commitments: Bell's theorem, no-go theorems (PBR, Frauchiger-Renner, Colbeck-Renner, Bong-Wiseman), the stochastic-quantum bridge, the necessity direction of the characterization theorem, the finiteness posit, computational implementability, the relationship to standard interpretations (MWI, Bohmian, QBism), the substratum-emergent operator distinction concern, circularity in the gap equation, the framework's epistemic status, and meta-objections about scope and credentials. Use as a reference resource for skeptical readers or for engaging the framework against specific objections.

The characterization of §4.3 concerns scalable uniform families of finite implementations. For a fixed physical realization, the total-finiteness posit ([Main] §1.2, §4.5) remains open and unadopted. Extending the holographic bound on the observed patch to all computationally relevant resources is the additional *patch-budget hypothesis*. The proposed width limit also needs a rate budget, a bridge from elementary substratum updates to classical sampling cost at the specified fidelity, and the hardness assumptions below.

It is natural to ask what additional axiom would close the gap between physical-substrate content and asymptotic complexity-class content. Several candidate forms are available, each illustrating the structural difficulty:

**Prerequisites.** This paper takes as established the following results from a companion work [Main]: (i) an observer embedded in a deterministic bijection on a finite configuration space, coupled to a hidden sector that is non-trivial (C1), record-persistent (C2), of sufficient memory capacity (C3 — with $N_H \gg N_V$ the comfortable regime), and read back (C4), has a reduced visible-sector description that is — in the memory-bearing sector that C1, C3 and C4 characterize — non-Markovian, and that universally admits a unitarily evolving fixed-basis quantum representation — the representation universal over finite laws ($S \iff D \iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}$), the necessity holding in the memory currency, with accessible non-Markovianity — the framework's finite-horizon visible-law memory notion, not generic quantum non-Markovianity — obtaining exactly when, for some accessible order $k$, every finite accessible horizon $K \geq k+1$ admits a deterministic realization with C1, C3 and C4, the readback at $k$ (a realization with C4 forces the memory by the readback lemma of [Main §2.3]; accessible memory yields such a realization by the finite-horizon process dilation of [Main §3.4]; both directions proved in prose), C2 lying outside that equivalence and the slow-bath form of its necessity for physical hidden sectors conditional on the hidden-sector mixing hypothesis, which the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis motivates, its persistence form holding without it, and full operational quantum theory approached at every finite test with its unique selection open; (ii) under the canonical measure of [Main] Lemma 3 — the invariant measure selected by maximal entropy — the emergent description is uniquely determined by the partition (partition-relativity); (iii) the emergent transition probabilities $T_{ij}(t)$ determine the Bohr-frequency set of the emergent Hamiltonian and, under the genericity hypotheses (G1)–(G4) of the phase-locking lemma or, without (G4), conditional on the classification hypothesis H-BG of §3.3, the emergent Hamiltonian itself up to a diagonal-unitary D-gauge, an energy origin, and one global antiunitary conjugation — the two-branch form of §3.3 — via the phase-locking lemma applied to continuous-time sampling. The technical bridge from P-indivisible classical stochastic processes on finite configuration spaces to unitary quantum evolution on finite Hilbert spaces is Barandes' stochastic-quantum correspondence [35, 36], used by the companion paper for compression and interpretation — the fixed-basis representation itself is supplied internally there ($S \iff D \iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}$). We treat these results as inputs and apply them to the cosmological horizon. For the cosmological application the Einstein constraints motivate a candidate C1 coupling, the Hubble-time mixing scale is an input for C2, and the boundary mode count gives a C3 capacity estimate for the chosen laboratory demand. The physical horizon application requires the realization of accessible coupling, persistence and capacity, and remains conditional on C4 (§2.2).

**The classical horizon temperature as a counting derivative, under H-count.** Under A1, restrict the finite total system to a conserved energy shell and let visible configuration $i$ carry energy $e_i$. If the boundary interaction is negligible at the shell scale, uniform counting gives $P(i)=\Omega_H(E-e_i)/\sum_j\Omega_H(E-e_j)$, so with $s_H=\ln\Omega_H$ and $\beta=s_H'(E)$, $P(i)\propto\exp[-\beta e_i+\tfrac12 s_H''(E)e_i^2+O(e_i^3)]$. Gibbs is the leading finite-bath marginal of uniform counting, classically. Under the hidden-sector condition **H-count** — that the total system is finite (A1) and that the energy-dependent entropy of the whole hidden sector at the shell scale is the boundary count, $s_H=\sigma A/\epsilon^2$ up to an energy-independent constant, the shell energy $E$ being the energy of the horizon first law and the deep hidden sector contributing no energy-dependent multiplicity and, by the choice of energy zero, no energy; S1–S4 do not supply it, their hidden capacity $\sim S_{\rm dS}$ fixing no entropy–energy slope — feeding in $dE=c^2\kappa\,dA/(8\pi G)$ gives $\partial s_H/\partial E=8\pi G\sigma/(c^2\kappa\epsilon^2)$ and hence $k_BT_{\rm micro}=(\partial s_H/\partial E)^{-1}=c^2\kappa\epsilon^2/(8\pi G\sigma)=k_BT_{\rm cl}$ — with no quantum mechanics, no KMS condition, no vacuum choice and no infinite bath. On the exact de Sitter calibration $E=c^4R/G$ and $s_H=4\pi\sigma G^2E^2/(c^8\epsilon^2)$, so $s_H''=\beta/E$ and the shell marginal is $P(i)\propto\exp[-\beta e_i+\beta e_i^2/(2E)]$: not exactly canonical, carrying the finite-reservoir correction $\delta_{\rm bath}\sim1/(4s_H)\sim10^{-123}$ at $s_H\sim10^{122}$. This is a second correction of the same spectacular smallness as the lattice-dispersion term $(\epsilon H/c)^2$, arising for an unrelated reason; the two should not be conflated.

**Classical microreversibility already gives the classical half.** With $M_i$ the shell microstates compatible with visible macrostate $i$, $N_i=|M_i|$ and $N_{ij}=|\{x\in M_i:\varphi(x)\in M_j\}|$, time-reversal invariance and time-reversal-even coarse states give a bijection between $i\to j$ and $j\to i$ trajectories, so $N_{ij}=N_{ji}$ and hence $N_iP_{ij}=N_jP_{ji}$ exactly. With $N_i=\Omega_H(E-e_i)$ this yields $\ln(P_{ij}/P_{ji})=-\beta_E(e_j-e_i)+\tfrac12 s_H''(E)(e_j^2-e_i^2)+\cdots$, with $\beta_E=s_H'(E)$ taking the boundary-count value above under H-count — the thermal rate ratio from finite deterministic reversible counting, with no quantum mechanics. Equating the two descriptions of the same observable rate ratio gives $\beta_E\Delta E=\tau_K\Delta\omega$ up to the two controlled corrections, hence $dE/d\omega=\tau_K/\beta_E$ in the infrared, and on a connected accessible sector $E_n=\hbar\omega_n+E_0$. The relation naive H-energy tried to assume emerges instead from thermal rate consistency. The remaining qualification is an identification of observables — that the classical shell transitions and the frequency-resolved detector transitions are the same operational transitions — which, if it requires arbitrary detector couplings, touches the coherent operational completion, which §3.3 characterizes, within complex matrix kinematics taken as given, by completion conditions whose physical sourcing is open.

**The gap equation in its cleanest form: $\hbar=\tau_K/\beta_E$.** Write the emergent evolution as $U_t=e^{-it\Omega_{\rm eff}}$ with $[\Omega_{\rm eff}]=\text{time}^{-1}$. Before the action scale is fixed the physical energy generator can only be $H_{\rm phys}=a_*\Omega_{\rm eff}$ for some universal $a_*$ with units of action; determining $a_*$ is what this section does, so it must not be set to $\hbar$ in advance. Classical horizon counting supplies an inverse energy, $\beta_E=\partial s_H/\partial E=8\pi G\sigma/(c^2\kappa\epsilon^2)$ under H-count. The emergent horizon state, conditional on H-spectrum, supplies an inverse time, $\tau_K=2\pi c/\kappa$. For a finite system a KMS state for evolution generated by $\Omega$ is Gibbs with exponent $-\tau_K\Omega$, so $e^{-\tau_K\Omega_{\rm eff}}=e^{-\beta_Ea_*\Omega_{\rm eff}}$ up to normalization, giving $\tau_K=\beta_Ea_*$ and
a_*=\frac{\tau_K}{\beta_E}=\frac{2\pi c/\kappa}{8\pi G\sigma/(c^2\kappa\epsilon^2)}=\frac{c^3\epsilon^2}{4G\sigma}=\hbar .

The action scale is exactly the conversion between an inverse-energy temperature obtained classically under H-count and an inverse-time KMS period obtained independently of it. No quantum mechanics enters the classical side and no $\hbar$ is inserted into $\tau_K$ beforehand.

**Why the classical shell state must not be identified with $e^{-\beta\hat H_{\rm eff}}$.** Suppose the configuration-diagonal shell state $\rho_{\rm shell}=\sum_ip_i|i\rangle\langle i|$ were required to be Gibbs for the emergent generator. Since $\rho_{\rm shell}>0$ the matrix logarithm is unique, so $\Omega_{\rm eff}=-\tau^{-1}\log\rho_{\rm shell}+\text{const}\,I$ is diagonal in the configuration basis, whence $|\langle j|e^{-it\Omega_{\rm eff}}|i\rangle|^2=\delta_{ij}$ — no configuration dynamics at all. That contradicts the generic phase-locking sector of [Main §3.2], where the energy eigenbasis overlaps every configuration state and $V=I$ is recorded as a nongeneric degeneracy. ### 7.3 Dark matter from entropy displacement
The boundary-density normalization of §7.2 motivates a proposal for the structured component. The displacement calculation uses the additional horizon and matter inputs below.

**Inherited conditions.** The chain below rests on the de Sitter temperature of §3.2, which is conditional: $T_{\rm dS}$ requires H-count (the hidden sector's energy-dependent entropy is its boundary count), H-slope (the infrared detailed-balance slope), H-frame (the preferred foliation is the comoving one), the H-Hawking conditions, local boost structure at the horizon and the symmetric detailed-balance rate ratio (§8.5), and the action-scale calibration is stated on an exact de Sitter horizon. The entropy-displacement chain of §7.3 therefore carries those conditions; the values of $a_0$ and $v^4$ in Steps 2–3 do not contain Step 1's $\Delta S$ and use $c$, $H$, $G$, $M_B$ and the imported factor. A second assumption is local to this section: writing $Q=M_Bc^2$ takes the entire rest energy of a static configuration to be delivered as heat to the boundary. That is a statement about how the emergent sector couples to the boundary — the same coupling map G3 names as open — and does not follow from (C1)'s requirement of nonzero cross-boundary interaction alone. A third input is imported: the dimensional factor converting the Hubble acceleration $cH$ into the critical acceleration is Verlinde's, not derived here (Step 2).

**Step 1: Entropy displacement (conditional on the above).** Baryonic matter $M_B$ is coupled to the boundary entropy through $H_{VB}$ (condition C1). The boundary is a thermal reservoir at $T_{\text{dS}} = \hbar H / (2\pi k_B)$ (§3.2, conditional). For a static matter configuration in gravitational equilibrium — a quasi-static process — the Clausius relation gives the entropy displacement:
$$\Delta S = \frac{M_B c^2}{k_B T_{\text{dS}}} = \frac{2\pi M_B c^2}{\hbar H}$$

This is the Clausius relation applied to the boundary reservoir: the boundary's entropy reduction is $Q/T$ for a reversible process, where $Q = M_B c^2$ and $T = T_{\text{dS}}$. This step uses the reversible static heat input.

**Step 2: The critical acceleration (conditional; imported).** The displaced entropy redistributes over the volume between the matter and the horizon. The proposed radial coupling uses the acceleration conversion in the Verlinde branch. The conversion is dimensional: in $d$ spacetime dimensions, the factor relating the natural Hubble acceleration scale $cH$ to the empirical MOND acceleration is $(d-3)/[(d-2)(d-1)]$. This derivation is due to Verlinde [20] (eq. 1.7), and follows from the interplay between volume-law entropy distributed over $(d-1)$ spatial dimensions and area-law entropy scaling with $(d-2)$ surface dimensions, together with the standard surface-density-to-acceleration relation via Gauss's law. In our universe ($d = 4$):
$$a_0 = \frac{(d-3)}{(d-2)(d-1)} \cdot cH = \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3} \cdot cH = \frac{cH}{6} = 1.09 \times 10^{-10} \; \text{m/s}^2 \quad (H_0 = 67.4\ \text{km s}^{-1}\text{Mpc}^{-1})$$

This is the MOND critical acceleration with no fitted parameter: $cH/6$ runs from $1.09 \times 10^{-10}$ m/s² at the Planck value of $H_0$ to $1.18 \times 10^{-10}$ m/s² at $H_0 = 73$, against the radial-acceleration-relation fit $g_\dagger = (1.20 \pm 0.02_{\rm rand} \pm 0.24_{\rm sys}) \times 10^{-10}$ m/s² [22], a ratio of $0.91$–$0.98$ that lies inside the stellar mass-to-light systematic. The factor 1/6 has dimensional origin — it is fixed by $d = 4$ together with the volume-vs-area entropy interplay — and is taken over from Verlinde's analysis rather than rederived from the substratum.

The OI framework's relation to Verlinde's derivation is that the volume-law entropy mechanism is placed on the framework's named conditions. In Verlinde's framework, the de Sitter states' non-thermalization ("memory effect") is hypothesized; in OI it is the persistence condition C2 ($\tau_B \gg \tau_S$) used as a physical input to the horizon application (§2.2). Whether this meets the consistency objection of [37] depends on the uncomputed relaxation kernel (§7.3); the published Verlinde–MOND consistency debate is relevant to the elasticity assumption in [20] and, through that kernel, to the present account.

**Step 3: The deep-MOND regime.** For baryonic acceleration $\ll a_0$, the assumed displacement law supplies the dominant radial acceleration, giving $g_{\text{total}} = \sqrt{g_B \cdot a_0}$ and rotation velocity:
$$v^2 = r \cdot g_{\text{total}} = \sqrt{GM_B \cdot cH/6} = \text{constant} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad v^4 = GM_B \cdot cH/6$$
This is the deep-MOND baryonic Tully-Fisher relation on the stated branch. Its normalization is compared with measured asymptotic rotation velocities and baryonic masses.
**Step 4: Radial interpolation.** For a static radial law, an entropy displacement potential is proposed with $g_D=-\nabla\Psi_D$. The following restrictions apply to the radial comparison:
(i) *No free parameters.* $g_D$ depends only on $g_B$ and $a_0 = cH/6$ — no halo-specific parameters, no fitting constants.
(ii) *Conservative.* $\nabla \times g_D = 0$, since $g_D$ derives from the entropy potential.
(iii) *Monotonic.* $\partial g_D / \partial g_B > 0$ — more baryonic mass produces more entropy displacement, hence more dark matter effect.
(iv) *Limits.* $g_D/g_B\to0$ for $g_B/a_0\to\infty$ (Newtonian), and $g_D\sim\sqrt{g_Ba_0}$ for $g_B/a_0\to0$ (deep-MOND regime).

**The sharp partition and constraint structure.** Lemma 2's product decomposition $\Gamma = \Gamma_V \times \Gamma_H$ is the kinematic phase space. In GR, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints restrict the physical phase space to a submanifold $\Gamma_{\text{phys}} \subset \Gamma_V \times \Gamma_H$ on which interior and exterior data are correlated. The recurrence-cycle P-indivisibility of [Main §2.3] carries over to a finite representative of the constraint surface, invariant under $\varphi$, with the hidden prior taken on each root's fiber: $\varphi$ restricted to $\Gamma_{\text{phys}}$ is a permutation of finite order $L$, so the rooted visible maps $K_t$, indexed by the visible values the surface admits, satisfy $K_{mL} = I$ for every $m \geq 0$, and a stochastic $\Lambda$ with $K_s \Lambda = K_{mL}$ for some $mL > s$ would be a stochastic right inverse of $K_s$, which the stochastic-inverse lemma of [Main §2.3] excludes unless $K_s$ is a permutation. Indivisibility across the recurrence cycle therefore needs only that some rooted visible map is not a permutation; it does not extend to accessible windows. At the cosmological horizon the boundary Hamiltonian and constraint structure motivate a candidate coupling. Accessible hidden-to-visible influence remains a condition [Main §1.3]. For systems other than the cosmological horizon, the fidelity of the product approximation determines the fidelity of the emergent quantum description.

Could quantum randomness arise because an observer sees only part of a deterministic world? Observational incompleteness (OI) investigates this possibility for embedded observers with finite resolution. In finite reversible models, every probability pattern over a finite observation window has a hidden deterministic realization, including the records of repeated fixed-basis quantum measurements. When the observed past helps predict the future beyond what the present reveals, every such realization must retain hidden predictive memory, with a minimum capacity. Under a common independent preparation of the hidden part, finite recurrence also forces a failure of step-by-step forecasting whenever a visible transition is uncertain. These results constrain representations of observations. Reproducing the full range of quantum experiments additionally requires a physical account of preparations, measurement choices, state changes and combined systems. The Born rule and that operational construction remain open. Vacuum energy and black-hole information illustrate further questions about the relation between global dynamics and accessible observations.

For the OI result, compare every possible visible start, preparing the hidden part with the same distribution independently of that start. One rule and one preparation then determine the whole family of forecasts. In a finite reversible world, all configurations eventually return to their starting values. If a visible step is uncertain, the family must fail to chain by this return [Main §2.3, Theorem (history readback + finite recurrence implies indivisibility)].

A fixed finite world with $N$ configurations can prepare at most $N$ distinguishable underlying states, so every experiment of the form "prepare, then measure" that it supports runs through distributions over those $N$ states [Main §3.4, Proposition (finite-substratum operational obstruction — classical-dimension form)]. A qubit, by contrast, has no such bound: reproducing the statistics of ever larger finite families of its preparations and measurements requires classical memory beyond every fixed bound [HKLP24, Thm 4; GH03]. Montina reports the corresponding result of Hardy that the underlying state set cannot be finite [Mon08, citing Har04].

The phrase "observation occurs" can be stated with more precision than a single undifferentiated axiom. Distilled, it is *two axioms*. **Axiom 1** is the evidential floor: tokened differentiation occurs — concrete differentiated content is *registered*, a this-not-that tokened from a locus against a remainder; equivalently, *embedded representation occurs*. It is indubitable, since to doubt it is itself to register a distinction from a locus — the cogito made precise, which is irreducibly perspectival: a registering from a locus, not a free-floating fact, and not a thinking subject — the primitive asserts no *I* (companion methodology paper, §2.3). Read this way, the primitive already contains three things that therefore need no separate derivation: a differentiation (the this-not-that), a locus that registers it (the observer of the Definition below), and the remainder it is registered against. The indubitability is the warrant available to whatever locus raises the doubt; the Definition covers every registering locus, and for a detector or a horizon that a registering occurs is a physical fact, not an indubitable one. The proper-part decomposition $V \subsetneq S$ — the observer embedded in a whole it does not exhaust — is accordingly constitutive of the primitive rather than a downstream posit: a registering that left no remainder would be the whole representing itself, not an observation. The relational structure follows from Axiom 1. A successor relation uses successive moments and a locus persisting across them. If the dynamics preserves registered records, states differing in those records have distinct successors. Per-moment finiteness of the visible configuration space (Lemma 1) follows from the finite-capacity clause of the Definition below. The bijective representative is a reconstruction choice motivated by observed near-unitarity. Total finiteness remains an open physical posit, not adopted, and one sufficient condition among those each result names (status Remark, §1.2 and ledger §4.5, item (ii)). One thing does not follow: that the differentiation *recurs* — that there is more than one moment for the dynamics to act across. This is **Axiom 2**: differentiation recurs, the temporal domain being the minimal such recurrence. Axiom 2 presupposes Axiom 1 (there is no recurrence of differentiation without differentiation) but is not derivable from it: a structure containing a single tokened differentiation and nothing further satisfies Axiom 1 while containing no recurrence, so no analysis of Axiom 1 alone can yield Axiom 2 — non-derivability by countermodel. The framework's foundation is therefore described not as a single axiom but as a *two-axiom observation base*: one indubitable claim, and one substantive posit that the first does not yield. The two invoke a single principle — tokened differentiation — and are thematically one; they are numerically two. The Definition and Lemmas below unpack this structure.

This definition formalizes three features implicit in the concept of observation: there is a whole ($S$), the observer is not the whole ($V \subsetneq S$), and the observer registers changes (coupling through $\varphi$). From this definition, three structural properties follow. The discrete-time model takes composition as a separate premise. Advancing the state by $t$ ticks and then by $s$ gives the update for $t+s$. This semigroup law yields iteration of the one-tick map, $x_t = \varphi^t(x_0)$ [45]. Phase flows provide a continuous-time example of compositional dynamics [44]. What distinguishes the present setting is not the existence of such a map but finiteness: the observer distinguishes finitely many visible configurations (Lemma 1), and on the bijective representative of the total-finiteness posit (§1.2 Remark, §4.5 ledger) the map acts on a finite $S$; finiteness of the visible sector (Lemma 1), not the dynamics, is the load-bearing commitment.

*Remark (the measure as a realization datum).* Lemma 3 fixes the canonical measure — invariant, maximal-entropy — and the framework's baseline transition matrices (§2.3) use it. On the selected bijective carrier $\mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H$ (Lemma 2) it is the uniform probability, with the uniform conditional law on $\mathcal{C}_H$ in each visible fibre; the counting probability on the eventual image of a non-bijective description (status Remark below) belongs to a different representative choice and in general has neither equal-size visible fibres nor a product form. It does not preclude structured preparations: a realization in the sense of §3.4 carries its own fixed hidden prior $\mu_H$ as part of the realization datum, and the emergent law is a function of $(\varphi, \text{partition}, \mu_H)$ — the same bijection and partition under different priors generally yield different visible laws (trivially: the two-state swap under uniform versus point-mass hidden priors). Partition-relativity statements are therefore relative to the declared measure; the counting measure is the default, not a constraint on representations.

*Remark (status of the early commitments).* Of the structure above, only finite visible resolution is a theorem (Lemma 1, from the finite-capacity clause of the Definition). The two axioms and the Definition leave the cardinality of the total configuration space open. The bijective substratum is a representation choice — the minimal recurrent bijective representative of the hidden dynamics, defined here for a finite system only: for a map $f$ on a finite set $X$ it is the restriction of $f$ to its eventual image $E = \bigcap_{n \ge 0} f^n(X)$, the set of states lying on cycles of $f$, on which $f$ is a bijection of finite order, $f^L = \text{id}$ on $E$ for some $L \ge 1$; no construction is given for an infinite $S$. Total finiteness of that representative is one sufficient condition for the results that use it, carried as item (ii) of the posit ledger (§4.5), the total-finiteness posit, an open hypothesis, not adopted; each such result names the hypotheses it consumes, and a weaker sufficient condition, where its sufficiency is proved, is stated with the result (§2.3, §3.2, §4.6); observed near-unitarity is the empirical input motivating the choice. The exact return $\varphi^L = \text{id}$ is a property of the finite representative; Axiom 2 asserts that differentiation recurs, not that every microstate returns. The physical reading of the characterization theorem — the identification of nature with a finite reversible substratum — is accordingly conditional on that representation choice, an empirically motivated reconstruction rather than a pure derivation; the law-level equivalence of §3.4 itself holds for every finite-horizon law. A finite factor adjoined to the hidden sector, prepared independently in a normalized state and evolved by its own permutation, with product dynamics, leaves every visible transition probability unchanged, because the visible coordinate of the product map does not depend on the added coordinate and the added prior has total mass one; the cardinality of such a deep sector is unobservable at the fixed visible/hidden interface. A deep sector that the dynamics couples to the remaining degrees of freedom, and an infinite hidden sector, are outside that statement, and this Remark makes no claim about the observability of their cardinality. Of the two finiteness statements, the following results use only that of Lemma 1: the stochastic-inverse lemma and the readback lemma (accessible conditional memory) of §2.3, and the equivalence of §3.4 with its process and intervention dilations, in which a finite hidden space is constructed, not assumed. The finite representative is used by the recurrence step of §2.3 (for whose P-indivisibility conclusion the near-return condition (NR) of §2.3 is a weaker sufficient condition; the exact return and its index $L$ are statements about the finite representative) and the results resting on it (recurrence-scale P-indivisibility, the CP-indivisibility theorem of §3.2, the all-time periodicity of a fixed realization in §3.4), by the eventual-image and surjectivity steps of the bijectivity argument below, by the counting measure of Lemma 3 and the uniform hidden prior that defines the baseline transition matrices, by the finite hidden space of the §3.2 setup, by the corner-occupancy claim of §3.1, by the finite-site presentation of the coupling-graph causal cone of §3.3, and by §4.6. The local-rule version of the cone in §3.3 applies on an arbitrary site set when each updated component reads a specified finite set of sites. The finite read sets give the cone in a graph containing their links. Injectivity (no merging of distinct states) holds, in the scope stated for each prong, by a two-pronged argument. Under the requirement that the dynamics preserve the observer's records, states carrying distinct registered records cannot share a successor. For states differing only in the hidden sector, a merge is either statistically observable or removable: a merge whose successor configurations differ visibly breaks the double stochasticity of the marginalized process at some step order (the marginal of a bijection under the uniform prior is doubly stochastic, since each set $\{x_j\} \times \mathcal{C}_H$ has exactly $|\mathcal{C}_H|$ preimages, §3.2, and unitary emergent statistics are unistochastic), so it is excluded wherever the observed statistics are of that doubly stochastic class under the uniform prior; a merge that leaves no statistical trace is removable for registered histories whose states lie in the *eventual image* $E$: any map on a finite set restricts to a bijection on $E$, at most one of two merged states lies in $E$, and on registered histories in $E$ the non-injective description coincides with its restriction to $E$. That representative is a restriction, not a factor, and the measure Lemma 3 assigns it is the counting measure on $E$, which conditioned on the visible value is uniform on the fibre of $E$ rather than on $\mathcal{C}_H$ and need not reproduce the uniform-prior statistics of the original description: on $\{0,1\} \times \{a,b,c\}$ with $f(0,a) = f(0,c) = (0,a)$, $f(0,b) = (1,a)$, $f(1,a) = (0,b)$ and $(1,b)$, $(1,c)$ fixed, $f$ has the visible process of the bijection that differs from it only in sending $(0,c)$ to itself, whose uniform-prior one-step matrix is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 2/3 & 1/3 \\ 1/3 & 2/3 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, while $E$ omits $(0,c)$ and the counting measure on $E$ gives $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 1/2 & 1/2 \\ 1/3 & 2/3 \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, which is not doubly stochastic. The uniform probability on the product carrier, used by Lemma 3, the baseline transition matrices and the §3.2 setup, and the counting probability on $E$ belong to different representative choices, and agreement of visible statistics under one does not transfer to the other without a separately verified measure-preserving correspondence. Either horn delivers a bijective substratum for the dynamics governing registered history in its scope, the second for registered states in $E$; the two prongs use different inputs — the first empirical (the observed statistics, in the uniform-prior doubly stochastic scope), the second structural (finiteness, for registered states in the eventual image). On a finite set, injectivity implies surjectivity, so on a finite representative $\varphi$ is a bijection. As for the measure on a finite representative: on the orbit of the actual microstate, the uniform measure is the unique $\varphi$-invariant measure; the selection among orbits is fixed by maximal entropy compatible with the observer's records — and an orbit of period $p$ makes at most $p$ states dynamically accessible. With preparation supported on that orbit, a proposed realization requiring more than $\log_2 p$ bits of predictive memory exceeds its capacity. The finite-law representation applies to laws with smaller memory requirements, including memoryless laws. The invariant counting measure, in the continuum limit, becomes the Liouville measure on $\Gamma$:

**(C1) Non-zero coupling.** $H_{\text{int}} \neq 0$: hidden degrees of freedom affect the visible evolution at some accessible step — the conditional law of some visible transition depends on the hidden state. A non-permutation one-step matrix $T$ is the cheapest sufficient *witness* (§2.3), not an equivalent: influence can hide at step one and surface later (the delayed-revival family, realized by the §3.4 construction; `review4_probes.py`). (Status: doubly anchored. Necessity — observed non-Markovian dynamics force C1: with no hidden influence at any accessible step, every visible transition is a fixed function of the visible present and the process is Markov (§3.4); directly observed memory effects in open-system dynamics certify the antecedent. Bell violation supplies a separate spatial-composite anchor only on the adopted ontic-parameter-dependent branch of §3.3; it does **not** by itself imply temporal P-indivisibility. Realization — the ADM boundary Hamiltonian and constraint correlations motivate a candidate horizon coupling. A C1 witness requires influence on an accessible visible conditional under the specified preparation. One-way influence can suffice for recurrence-cycle indivisibility (§3.4, non-permutation witness). Dependency — C1 is *not independent of C4*: a readback gap requires hidden mediation, so any realization satisfying C4 satisfies C1, and zero-coupling realizations exhibit no gap at any order, certified by exhaustive enumeration at $(n_V, |\mathcal{C}_H|) = (2,2), (2,3), (3,2)$ in `primitive_probes.py`. C1 is retained as a separately checkable condition — the adopted Bell branch independently requires Bell-relevant cross-wing coupling, while C4 already forces hidden mediation — not as an independent postulate.)

**Theorem statement.** The claims divide into three exact layers and one explicitly conditional extension. **(1) Representation equivalence:** on every finite accessible horizon, the stochastic laws $S$, their finite reversible deterministic realizations $D$, and fixed-basis unitary/Born representations $Q_{\mathrm{fb}}$ are the same class, $S\iff D\iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}$ (§3.4). **(2) Readback content:** C4 is not needed for the existence of a quantum representation; it is what makes the OI sector nontrivial. C4 forces conditional memory in the visible law and readout-relevant hidden predictive memory in every faithful completion (§3.4); indivisibility somewhere in the recurrence cycle of a fixed finite reversible representative follows from any non-deterministic visible step, including in laws that are Markov on every accessible window, and does not require C4; with a full-support visible prior it is equivalent to memory at some order below the recurrence time, which an observer reaches only when that order is accessible, as C4 asserts (§2.3). C1 follows as a necessary diagnostic of the mediation, and C3 holds in every faithful realization by the capacity bound; C2-structural, the persistence of the record to readback, holds by reversibility in every bijective realization and constrains coarse-grained descriptions of the hidden sector, with C2-slow one physical mechanism. **(3) Reverse finite realization:** every finite stochastic law, including every finite quantum record, has a finite reversible OI realization; bounded quantum instrument families are uniformly realizable to arbitrary finite accuracy for a fixed initial state with supplied quantum data (§3.4). **(4) Full operational extension:** one common *standard quantum instrument/composite theory* for all coherent interventions is obtained, on a finite carrier with complex matrix kinematics taken as given, exactly under the five completion conditions of §3.4. Under the substratum's stated interventions (its finite bijective read-write dynamics and the phase intervention), (iv), full reversible control, is not supplied (kernel: `substratumGen_not_control` in `OIBridge/StructuralClosure.lean`, on the two-state carrier); whether an extended OI mechanism supplies it, and which of the other conditions the substratum supplies, are open. Bell is a separate constraint rather than one of those conditions: for a response-complete deterministic completion that records a $\pm1$ outcome in every run, measurement independence plus ontic parameter independence would force $|S_{\rm CHSH}|\le2$, so the Bell-violating branch adopted in §3.3 retains measurement independence and relinquishes ontic parameter independence with operational no-signaling required.

By Lemma 1 the visible sector is finite; under the total-finiteness posit (§1.2 Remark, §4.5 ledger) the hidden sector is also finite — configuration spaces $\mathcal{C}_V$ and $\mathcal{C}_H$ (the discrete counterparts of $\Gamma_V$ and $\Gamma_H$). On these finite sets:

**Theorem.** *Let $\mathcal{C}_V$ and $\mathcal{C}_H$ be finite sets with $|\mathcal{C}_V| \geq 2$, and let $\varphi: \mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H \to \mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H$ be a bijection. Define:*
$$T_{ij} = \frac{|\{h \in \mathcal{C}_H : \pi_V(\varphi(x_i, h)) = x_j\}|}{|\mathcal{C}_H|}$$
*and the $k$-step matrix $T^{(k)}_{ij}$ by applying $\varphi^k$. If $T$ is not a permutation matrix, then the process is P-indivisible.*

*Proof.* Uses total variation distance $d(p, q) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_k |p_k - q_k|$. P-divisibility $\implies$ $d(p(t), q(t))$ non-increasing for all initial $p, q$ [4, 5] (a stochastic divisor is a total-variation contraction); the proof below uses only this direction, in contrapositive form. The converse is *false*: monotonicity constrains the divisor only on the image directions $(\delta_i - \delta_j)T(1,0)$, not on the extreme points of the zero-sum ball, and explicit stochastic pairs exist whose unique divisor $T(1,0)^{-1}T(2,0)$ carries a negative entry — no stochastic divisor, hence P-indivisible — while $d$ is non-increasing for every $p, q$; one such pair is strictly contracting at $n = 2$ and one lies in the doubly stochastic class at $n = 3$ (`translation_probes.py`). Monotonicity is therefore a necessary, not sufficient, condition for P-divisibility, and is not used as a criterion anywhere below.
*Step 1 (Recurrence).* $\varphi$ bijective on a finite set $\Rightarrow$ $\exists N: \varphi^N = \text{id}$. Thus $T^{(N)} = I$ and $d(\delta_i T^{(N)}, \delta_j T^{(N)}) = 1$ for $i \neq j$.
*Step 2 (Strict contraction).* $T$ not a permutation $\Rightarrow$ $\exists i, j, l$: $T_{il} > 0$ and $T_{jl} > 0$. Then:
$$d(\delta_i T, \delta_j T) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_k |T_{ik} - T_{jk}| < 1$$
*Step 3.* $d(\delta_i T^{(1)}, \delta_j T^{(1)}) < 1 = d(\delta_i T^{(N)}, \delta_j T^{(N)})$: non-monotonic, hence P-indivisible. $\square$

The theorem requires only bijective dynamics (Lemma 3) and a non-permutation one-step matrix $T$, under the uniform hidden prior that defines $T$; (C1) acting at the first step supplies one, and (C1) acting only at later steps does not (§1.3). Lemma 1 gives the finite visible space; the hidden space is finite under the total-finiteness posit (§1.2, §4.5).

*Corollary (near-return).* *Let $\mathcal{C}_V$ be finite with $|\mathcal{C}_V| \geq 2$, let $\rho$ be a probability on a measurable space $H$, shared by every root, let $F$ be a measurable map of $\mathcal{C}_V \times H$, and let $\Gamma_t(a, b) = \rho\{h : \pi_V F^t(a, h) = b\}$. If $\Gamma_s$ is not a permutation matrix, some roots $a \neq b$ and value $x$ have $m = \min(\Gamma_s(a, x), \Gamma_s(b, x)) > 0$. Assume, as a hypothesis of this result and not adopted, the near-return condition (NR) for such a pair: some $n > s$ has $(1 - \Gamma_n(a, a)) + (1 - \Gamma_n(b, b)) < m$. Then the rooted family is not P-divisible on $\{0, \ldots, n\}$.* *Proof.* Each $\Gamma_t$ is row-stochastic because $\rho$ is a probability. If the $|\mathcal{C}_V|$ rows of $\Gamma_s$ had pairwise disjoint supports, the supports would partition the $|\mathcal{C}_V|$ columns into singletons and $\Gamma_s$ would be a permutation matrix; so two rows $a \neq b$ share a column $x$, and $m > 0$. Then $d(\Gamma_s(a), \Gamma_s(b)) \leq 1 - m$, while testing the event $\{a\}$ gives $d(\Gamma_n(a), \Gamma_n(b)) \geq \Gamma_n(a, a) - \Gamma_n(b, a) \geq 1 - (1 - \Gamma_n(a, a)) - (1 - \Gamma_n(b, b)) > 1 - m$. A row-stochastic $\Lambda$ with $\Gamma_n = \Gamma_s \Lambda$ would not increase the total variation distance between rows (the contraction stated at the start of the proof above), so none exists. $\square$ On a finite representative Step 1 supplies the condition (NR) at every multiple of $N$ exceeding $s$. The condition (NR) needs no finite hidden space, invariant law, bijection or period $N$; $n$ is any time after $s$ at which its inequality holds.

*Scope.* This is a global recurrence-cycle result. It does **not** say that C4 forces P-indivisibility on every accessible short-time window; the XOR control remains a counterexample to that stronger statement. With a full-support visible prior the hypothesis and the conclusion coincide on the representative: a readback gap at some order below $L$ — two positive-probability histories with a common endpoint and different next-step laws, equivalently $M_k > 0$ for some $k < L$ — a non-permutation $\Gamma_s$ for some $0 < s < L$, and failure of P-divisibility on $\{0, \ldots, L\}$ are equivalent. Without a gap below $L$ the law on $\{0, \ldots, L\}$ is Markov with kernels $Q_k$, $\Gamma_t = Q_0 \cdots Q_{t-1}$, and $I = \Gamma_L = \Gamma_s (Q_s \cdots Q_{L-1})$ makes each $\Gamma_s$ a permutation by the lemma; if every $\Gamma_s$ is a permutation, $\Gamma_s^{-1}\Gamma_t$ is a stochastic divisor. Full support enters only in the first of these steps: otherwise a non-permutation row may belong to a root of visible probability zero while the realized law has no gap. For every visible prior, a non-deterministic visible step — $P(X_{t+1} \mid X_t = x)$ not a point mass for some positive-probability $x$ — makes some $\Gamma_s$ a non-permutation, so the recurrence-cycle indivisibility holds for every representative with such a step, laws that are Markov on every accessible window included. Under a full-support prior, the gap it is equivalent to may lie at any order below the recurrence time; (C4) and condition (ii) of §3.4 require an accessible order. The equivalence is a property of the representative's rooted law over its whole recurrence cycle; an observer's statistics are its restriction to accessible windows, and on them the memory is witnessed only by a gap at an accessible order. What (C4) adds within accessible windows is the positive conditional memory of the readback lemma below. Without a finite representative the index-free form holds under full support of the visible prior, (FS), with the root drawn independently of the hidden prior, and, for the step from (b) to (c), the near-return condition (NR), both assumed as hypotheses of this form and not adopted, one direction at a time. (a) A readback gap at some finite order $k$ gives (b) some $\Gamma_s$, $1 \leq s \leq k$, that is not a permutation, by the first half of the proof above with $\min(k, L-1)$ replaced by $k$, which uses no return. (b) gives (c), the family not P-divisible on $\{0, \ldots, n\}$ for some $n$, by the corollary (near-return), when the near-return condition (NR) holds for an overlapping pair of rows of that $\Gamma_s$, assumed as a hypothesis of this implication and not adopted. (c) gives (a): if no order below $n$ has a gap, the law on $\{0, \ldots, n\}$ is Markov with one-step matrices $Q_j$ (rows of zero-probability states chosen stochastic), every root has positive probability under full support (FS), so each row of $\Gamma_t$ is a conditional law of that Markov process and $\Gamma_t = \Gamma_s (Q_s \cdots Q_{t-1})$ for all $s < t \leq n$, and the family is P-divisible on $\{0, \ldots, n\}$. The bound below $L$ and the horizon $\{0, \ldots, L\}$ are statements about the finite representative.

*Routed readback.* The realization clause of (C4) (§1.3), a visible-history record written into the hidden state and routed back into later visible conditionals, has two formalizations on the rooted maps above, which differ in the hidden variable that carries the record at the storage time. Both fix roots $a \neq b$, times $0 < w \leq s < t \leq K$ and a visible value $x$, and require four clauses: a write, some seed $h$ with $\mu_H(h) > 0$ for which $\varphi^w(a, h)$ and $\varphi^w(b, h)$ have different hidden components; a store, $\Gamma_s(a, x) > 0$, $\Gamma_s(b, x) > 0$ and different root-conditioned hidden laws at $(s, x)$ for the two roots; a read, those two hidden laws placed beside $x$ and evolved for $t - s$ steps giving different visible laws at $t$; and a reappearance, $\Gamma_t(a, \cdot) \neq \Gamma_t(b, \cdot)$. In the storage-time reading the hidden law is that of the hidden state at the storage time, $\mathrm{Law}(H_s \mid X_s = x, X_0 = a)$; in the seed-conditioned reading it is that of the initial hidden state, $\mathrm{Law}(H_0 \mid X_s = x, X_0 = a)$. Under either reading, the rooted family is not P-divisible on $\{0, \ldots, n\}$ for every $n > s$ with $\Gamma_n = I$, and so for some $n$, because $(\Gamma_t)$ is periodic and $\Gamma_0 = I$ (kernel: `routedAtStorage_forces_return_indivisibility`, `routedAtStorage_forces_indivisible_somewhere` in `OIBridge/PhysicalC4StorageReadback.lean` for the storage-time reading; `routed_forces_return_indivisibility`, `routed_forces_indivisible_somewhere` in `OIBridge/PhysicalC4Discharge.lean` for the seed-conditioned reading; the period and the root identity are `rootedMap_periodic` and `rootedMap_zero` in `OIBridge/RootedClassification.lean`). Both proofs use only the two positivity conditions of the store clause, so both conclusions are instances of the overlap-and-return theorem, and the horizon reached is a return of the rooted map, not an accessible window. Neither reading implies the other: each holds at $K = 2$ on an exhibited finite reversible realization on which the other fails at $K = 2$ (kernel: `storageReadback_not_implies_routedReadback`, `routedReadback_not_implies_storageReadback`). Whether the clause holds at a physical cut, in either reading, is not established (§1.3).

The recurrence argument establishes P-indivisibility across the recurrence cycle. The readback lemma below shows that a readback gap at an accessible order produces conditional memory on observable timescales; that is a property of the multi-time law and does not by itself make the rooted family P-indivisible on those windows (Scope, above). A sufficient further condition is a revival of distinguishability within the window: two roots whose rooted laws coincide, or are closer, at an earlier time and differ more at a later one.

**Role of (C2)–(C4).** The finite-recurrence argument and the readback lemma are independent: the former establishes P-indivisibility from a non-permutation one-step witness and finiteness alone, at the recurrence time, or from a non-permutation rooted map and the near-return condition (NR) of §2.3, assumed in its place and not adopted, without finiteness of the hidden sector; the latter locates observable conditional memory inside accessible windows, which does not by itself make the rooted family P-indivisible there. (C2) keeps stored history alive between couplings; (C3) provides the room to store it; (C4) is the reading of it — and only the reading produces memory an observer can measure.

**Weak-coupling and fast-bath regimes.** Known P-divisible systems with non-zero coupling are not counterexamples to the recurrence theorem, whose hypotheses they do not meet. The Jaynes-Cummings model with Lorentzian spectral density is P-divisible when dissipation dominates coupling, and the Davies-Merkli Markovian convergence theorem applies in the Born-Markov limit; both couple to a continuum reservoir, so the finite recurrence the theorem uses is absent. Both sit in the fast-bath regime ($\tau_B \ll \tau_S$), where (C2) fails in its timescale form. The recurrence theorem uses no form of (C2), deriving recurrence-cycle P-indivisibility from a non-permutation rooted map and finite order alone; in particular the timescale form of (C2) is not necessary for it in a finite bijective realization, where (C2-structural) holds by reversibility (§1.3). What the §3.4 physical-memory theorem bounds is conditional memory, not P-divisibility: under the mixing hypothesis, for $\varepsilon \leq 1 - 1/n_V$, a fast bath leaves at most $2[\varepsilon \log(n_V - 1) + h(\varepsilon)]$ of it, with $\varepsilon$ the residue of relaxation at the coupling time.

**Continuous spectra and the finite-substratum commitment.** Lemma 1 fixes the visible configuration space as finite, and the Barandes correspondence as applied here produces an emergent Hilbert space of finite dimension. Standard quantum mechanics makes heavy use of continuous-spectrum observables — position on $\mathbb{R}^3$, momentum, continuous-spectrum scattering — which strictly require infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and unbounded self-adjoint operators. The framework's position on this is that continuous spectra are the infrared limit of the discrete spectrum produced by Lemma 1, not a deeper reality that the framework fails to capture. The quantitative separation is extreme: for a visible sector bounded by the cosmological horizon, of radius $L_H$, and an assumed discreteness scale $\epsilon$ of the order of the Planck length $l_p$, the number of distinguishable positions is $|\mathcal{C}_V| \sim (L_H/\epsilon)^3 \sim 10^{183}$, and no independent continuous-spectrum prediction is needed or claimed. Calvo [13] extends the Barandes correspondence to countable-infinite dimensions for completeness, but the finite-dim correspondence is the load-bearing one for the framework — every result in §2–§3 other than the infinite-region completion (§3.2, §3.4), which is assembled from finite-region stages, runs on finite configuration spaces: Lemma 1 for the visible sector, with the total-finiteness posit (§1.2 Remark, §4.5) where a result also needs the hidden sector finite; the near-return corollary of §2.3, the index-free form of §2.3 under (FS) and (NR), and the remark of §3.2 under the condition (IP) take a measurable hidden space.

**Setup.** The finite configuration spaces $\mathcal{C}_V = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}$ and $\mathcal{C}_H = \{h_1, \ldots, h_m\}$ (Lemma 1 for $\mathcal{C}_V$; $\mathcal{C}_H$ under the total-finiteness posit, §1.2, §4.5) embed into Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_V = \mathbb{C}^n$ and $\mathcal{H}_H = \mathbb{C}^m$ via $|i\rangle \leftrightarrow x_i$ and $|k\rangle \leftrightarrow h_k$. This introduces no quantum postulates: it is the canonical identification of probability distributions on a finite set with diagonal density matrices. The uniform hidden prior of this section is the uniform probability on the product carrier $\mathcal{C}_V \times \mathcal{C}_H$ of a bijection; the counting probability on the eventual image of a non-bijective description (§1.2) is a different measure, to which statements made under this prior do not transfer without a separately verified measure-preserving correspondence.

*Remark (three notions, kept apart).* Three distinct things travel under nearby names, and this paper uses them in fixed senses. (1) **Accessible finite-horizon memory**, equivalently conditional past–future dependence in the visible law: this is the framework's own notion, what the characterization theorem is about, what $M_t > 0$ measures, and what (C1), (C3) and (C4) diagnose on a finite horizon. Where this paper writes "accessible non-Markovianity" it means exactly this and says nothing about a quantum channel. (2) **Stochastic P-indivisibility**: failure of stochastic divisibility of the visible population law, which on one fixed finite reversible representative is what the recurrence-scale theorem delivers — resting on recurrence together with a non-permutation rooted map, not on (C1), (C3) and (C4) alone. (3) **Generic quantum non-Markovianity**: an open-system notion whose content depends on which quantum divisibility or backflow criterion is adopted. No unconditional implication among the three is asserted here. The two preceding remarks give the exact conditions under which (2) constrains a quantum intermediate map, and the Hadamard family shows that outside the diagonal-preserving class (2) and (3) come apart.

**Dependency scope of the correspondence.** The equivalence theorem of §3.4 fixes the framework's exposure to the correspondence precisely, and it is narrower than earlier versions of this paper claimed. *In-house:* the finite-horizon equivalence $S \iff D \iff Q_{\mathrm{fb}}$ — existence of a fixed-basis unitary Born representation for every finite-horizon law, the framework's own processes included, by the permutation unitary of any realization — together with the fixed-$\hat{H}$ lemma, the phase-locking gauge, and the universal hidden-memory theorem. *Imported, under (T):* the source's $\leq n^3$ dilation bound for its finite-configuration class, which the per-time form on dimension $n^2$ (§3.1) does not need, and the interpretive apparatus that travels with it (basis independence, the general-observable reading). *Additional, with neither route supplying it:* the operational instrument algebra and coherent preparation — supplied exactly by the five operational completion conditions of the characterization of §3.4, none of which bare finite OI provides — and representation consistency across growing horizons (the obstruction theorem of §3.4). A failure of the correspondence would therefore cost the framework the interpretive apparatus, and nothing else: existence of the representation, its per-time form on dimension $n^2$ (§3.1), the equivalence, and the necessity results are internal. P-indivisibility appears nowhere in this division of labor — it gates neither membership in the source's class nor the representation's existence (§3.4, Remark) — and its role is confined to nontriviality at the recurrence scale and to the Bell-class constructions of §3.3.

**Operational-reconstruction route: target conditions and the outstanding bridge.** Both routes above are constructive: they exhibit quantum mechanics as a description of the marginalized process. The reconstruction theorems [Hardy, arXiv:quant-ph/0101012 (2001); Masanes and Müller, New J. Phys. **13**, 063001 (2011); Chiribella, D'Ariano and Perinotti, Phys. Rev. A **84**, 012311 (2011)] derive quantum theory from operational axiom sets. The physical layer supplies two useful ingredients: every fixed finite representative has finite predictive dimension, and the substratum dynamics admits reversible dilations. Neither statement by itself discharges the corresponding hypothesis for an **exact operational completion**. **Lemma (non-permutation witness).** *For the finite bijective model of §3.2 with its common uniform hidden prior, a non-permutation one-step matrix $T$ witnesses hidden-to-visible influence at the first step (C1). The rooted family fails P-divisibility by the return.*

*Proof.* The common uniform prior makes $T$ doubly stochastic, so a non-permutation $T$ has a nondegenerate row and hence hidden-to-visible influence. Section 2.3's finite-recurrence argument rules out a stochastic divisor from the first step to the return. $\square$

*Proposition (finite-substratum operational obstruction — classical-dimension form).* Fix one realization: a substratum of $N < \infty$ ontic configurations with its observation map. Its full prepare-and-measure behavior factors as $B = \Xi M$ — preparations as columns of a column-stochastic $M$ (distributions over the $N$ ontic states), effects as rows of $\Xi \in [0,1]^{\,\cdot \times N}$ — so every behavior matrix the realization generates has nonnegative factorization through $N$ states. For the qubit this is impossible uniformly: qubit prepare-measure behaviors have PSD rank $2$ but nonnegative rank growing without bound over finite prepare–measure sets, so for every $N$ there is a finite qubit experiment no $N$-state model reproduces exactly (Heinosaari–Kerppo–Leppäjärvi–Plávala [55]; an alternative route under procedural-independence assumptions: Garner–Müller [56]). The factorization interface assumed is the ordinary preparation $\to$ finite ontic system $\to$ measurement one; the same work's coordinated version extends the obstruction against finite shared coordination between the sides [55]. Hence no fixed finite realization is exactly operationally equivalent to even a single qubit's full theory — the elementary factorization half proved here, the unboundedness imported. The obstruction is independent of C1–C4 and of horizon growth. It does not touch the equivalence theorem — there the realization is chosen per finite-horizon law, and a fixed finite table of statistics always has one — and it is precisely why the equivalence carries its subscript. $\square$
